name: Lena Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can give me the public answer and the private one. Could you start by walking me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the live-line crew down by the port, which means we work on lines while they're still switched on, so the factories and the cranes don't lose power. Rubber gloves up to the shoulder, insulated sticks, a lot of slow, careful moves. A normal day is one big job, like swapping an insulator on a line feeding the container terminal, and a lot of planning beforehand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's precise. One wrong move and it's very bad, so you're completely in the moment. The hard part is that I'm on the lower pay scale for the port district and I've only got about three weeks of money saved, mostly because I moved flats this year and bought a used electric car. It's me and my dog Pixel in a one-bedroom near the docks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to prep job plans, to check clearance distances, to summarise safety bulletins, even to edit the short videos I post about line work. I've got about eight thousand followers, mostly other lineworkers and people who think it looks cool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, people just expected magic. I'd probably make a video about how I actually use it on a job, the boring practical stuff. At work most people wouldn't care either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit boring. I was hoping it'd shake things up and I'd get into something new. But it's fine, live-line work is safe and I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep using the tools I already use. Grow the videos a bit, maybe get a small sponsor for gloves or tools, which would help with the cushion. Save for a better car battery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a sponsor mean for you financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even a couple of hundred a month would double what I save. Right now my cushion is basically Pixel's vet fund and whatever's left of the car payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would it feel flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like new things. I'd been reading about the robot arms some companies use for live-line work, and I wanted to be the one who runs it here. If nothing changes, that stays a someday.

S0.say: It's still useful, people just expected magic. She'd make a video showing how she actually uses AI on a job.
S0.think: It's a bit boring, because she hoped for a shake-up that would lead her into something new. Live-line work stays safe, and she likes it.
S0.do: Keeps using the tools she already uses and grows her videos, aiming for a small glove or tool sponsor worth a couple of hundred a month. Saves toward a better car battery.
S0.quote: Right now my cushion is basically Pixel's vet fund and whatever's left of the car payment.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is the opposite of fearful: she's mildly disappointed that nothing changes. Her savings are thin from a move and a used car, not from carelessness. Her videos are a real, small side income in waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when it gets interesting, and people who learn fast will do well. I'd make videos about the new tools, honestly. At work I'd be the one volunteering for every trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Live-line robot arms already exist. If our company brings one in, I want to be the one operating it from the truck. The guys who refuse to touch it will get left behind, and that's sad, but it's not my call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd go to my supervisor and ask to be on any pilot for robot or drone tools. I'd do every online course I could find on robotic live-line systems in the evenings. I'd make videos about the transition, which might actually grow the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Henri. He's fifty-two, the best stick man I've ever seen. He says he'll retire before he touches a joystick. I'd hate to see someone that good on the sticks pushed out by someone like me who's just better at video games.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if people like Henri lost out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's just how it goes. The company has to stay up to date. I'd try to help Henri learn it, but if he won't, he won't.

S1.say: This is when it gets interesting, and fast learners will do well. She'd make videos about the new tools and volunteer for every trial.
S1.think: It's good for her: live-line robot arms already exist and she wants to run one from the truck. Those who refuse will be left behind, which is sad but not her call.
S1.do: Asks her supervisor for a place on any robot or drone pilot and takes evening online courses on robotic live-line systems. Makes videos about the change to grow her account.
S1.quote: I'd hate to see someone that good on the sticks pushed out by someone like me who's just better at video games.
S1.fieldNote: She wants to be the operator of the robot that does her job. She blames no one for people being left behind, but feels a real pang about Henri. Her pragmatism can sound a little cool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, adapt or get flattened. That's what I'd say on video, probably. At work I'd try to be less blunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Three weeks of money, and if AGI can run the robot arms itself, there's no operator job either. My edge is learning fast, but if the machine learns faster, what's my edge?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. Sell the electric car, which would clear the loan and leave a bit. Look at robotics companies in the big city, three hours away, for anything, installation, testing, support. I'd move there with Pixel if I got something, even a room in a shared house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But wired, too, like before a big job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your followers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, that I'm scrambling like everyone else. I'd film myself packing up my gloves, because that's the honest video. Maybe that'd help someone feel less alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge is learning fast. How would you know it's not enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't, not right away. I'd find out by getting turned down. I think I'd try three or four things in the first year and see which one stuck.

S2.say: It's here, so adapt or get flattened. That's what she'd say on video, though she'd put it more gently to her crew at work.
S2.think: She's worried: with three weeks of money and AGI able to run robot arms itself, even the operator job disappears. Her edge is learning fast, but the machine may learn faster.
S2.do: Sells her electric car to clear the loan and applies to robotics companies three hours away for installation, testing or support work. Moves there with her dog into a shared house if she gets something.
S2.feel: Anxious, but wired like before a big job.
S2.quote: I'd film myself packing up my gloves, because that's the honest video.
S2.fieldNote: Her confidence takes its first knock here: being a fast learner may not matter. She'd still move quickly, selling the car and leaving town. Her plan to film the honest version stood out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a real move if you start now. I'd make videos about what people in the trade could retrain into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. Enough to get proper robotics qualifications and maybe work for one of the companies making live-line robots, as the person who knows what the job actually feels like. That's rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd sign up for a part-time robotics technician diploma, online with some weekends in the city. I'd keep working live-line to pay for it. I'd push the videos harder and try to get a sponsor, and save whatever that brings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean, the person who knows what the job feels like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot companies have engineers who've never been near a live line. They need someone who knows what it's like when the wind picks up and the line starts swinging two metres from your face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between two years and five for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm grabbing anything. Five years, I can actually build a path. I'd still be nervous, but I'd feel like I'm steering.

S3.say: Five years is enough to make a real move if you start now. She'd make videos about what people in the trade could retrain into.
S3.think: Five years suits her: she could get robotics qualifications and join a company making live-line robots, bringing rare knowledge of how the work actually feels.
S3.do: Signs up for a part-time robotics technician diploma, online with some weekends in the city, paid by live-line work. Pushes her videos to win a sponsor and saves what it brings.
S3.quote: They need someone who knows what it's like when the wind picks up and the line starts swinging two metres from your face.
S3.fieldNote: She frames her field experience as something robot makers lack. More time lets her steer rather than grab. The videos keep coming back as both income and identity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. Don't sit around. I'd probably make a whole series about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven, I'd have done robotics, maybe worked for one of the robot companies, maybe even started something of my own. The end point's the same, but I'd have done a lot by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics diploma over two or three years. I'd keep the videos going and turn them into a small business, maybe training content for new lineworkers. If I ever had spare money, I'd put a bit into shares in the robot companies, since that's where things are going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I'd have time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Shares, with a thin cushion. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not now. Maybe in year four or five, once the side stuff is paying. I'd rather own a tiny piece of the robot than just fight it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the end, when AGI arrives? Where would you be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe nowhere useful, like everyone else. But I'd have had ten good years of trying things, and that counts for something.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so use it and don't sit around. She'd make a whole video series about it.
S4.think: She'd be fine at 37, having studied robotics and perhaps worked for a robot company or started her own business. The end point is the same, but she'd have done a lot by then.
S4.do: Takes the robotics diploma over two or three years and turns her videos into a small training-content business for new lineworkers. Puts spare money into robot company shares from year four or five.
S4.feel: Calm, with time to get ready.
S4.quote: I'd rather own a tiny piece of the robot than just fight it.
S4.fieldNote: This is the only scenario where she talks about owning part of the change rather than surviving it. She admits she doesn't know where she'd be at the end. The ten years feel like a runway to her, not a countdown.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time for my usual trick, which is learning faster than everyone. What would help is quick, free training in the city for people from the trades, with somewhere to live while you do it. Housing is the thing that stops people like me moving.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the danger. People forget how risky this job is. If a robot takes the live-line work, fewer people get burned, and I'd take that trade even if it costs me my job.

headlineQuote: If a robot takes the live-line work, fewer people get burned, and I'd take that trade even if it costs me my job.
portrait: Lena is a 27-year-old live-line worker who works on switched-on lines feeding the port's factories and cranes, using AI every day and posting short videos about her work. She lives with her dog in a one-bedroom near the docks, with about three weeks of savings after a move and a used electric car. She finds AI Plateau slightly flat and welcomes Steady Disruption, keen to operate the robot arms herself. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious because her edge, learning fast, might not be enough, so she'd sell the car and move to the city. Given five or ten years, she'd study robotics, build her videos into a business and even want a small stake in the robot companies.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be no time for her usual advantage of learning faster than everyone else.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, free training in the city for people from the trades, with somewhere to live while they study.
